survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This factsheet reports PISA 2022 results for Poland using OECD’s PISA 2022 Database and published tables. The note does not specify whether analysts applied student/sampling weights or replicate weights (e.g., BRR/jackknife) when producing the reported percentages and mean estimates. For PISA, estimates are typically produced under a complex two-stage sampling design (students within schools) and should be computed with the provided sampling weights and appropriate variance estimation to obtain correct uncertainty intervals. Because this document is a published results factsheet rather than a re-analysis with microdata, the manuscript does not report any weight variable names or replicate design settings; users should follow the OECD PISA technical documentation for the correct weight and variance estimation approach.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This document is a results factsheet that reports descriptive PISA outcomes (means, proficiency-level shares, and trends) rather than training or estimating predictive models on student microdata. As such, it does not describe plausible-value (PV) generation/combining or missing-data imputation procedures in the way an empirical PV-based analysis paper would. The factsheet also does not provide enough methodological detail to attribute a specific PV or missing-data handling strategy to the reported estimates.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analytic subset reported for Poland includes 15-year-old students who completed the PISA 2022 assessment in mathematics, reading, or science, with 6011 students in 240 schools. The factsheet does not describe additional exclusions beyond the standard PISA data collection and quality checks; it states that in Poland all data met PISA quality standards and were considered fit for reporting.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD PISA 2022 Poland factsheet summarizes how 15-year-old students in Poland performed in mathematics, reading, and science, and how results changed relative to earlier PISA cycles (notably 2018 and 2012). It reports mean performance trends and proficiency-level distributions (e.g., shares at Level 2+ and Level 5/6), alongside gaps by socio-economic status (ESCS international quintiles and within-country top/bottom quarters) and gender differences. The assessment design uses two two-hour tests per student, with different students receiving different subject combinations and item sets, plus a background questionnaire for students and a principal questionnaire for school context. The factsheet notes that PISA 2022 was delayed to 2022 due to COVID-19 and that some countries/economies may have sampling-standard issues (Poland’s data met quality standards). Reported uncertainty is expressed via 95% confidence intervals, and comparisons are made against the OECD average and selected comparison countries.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is not an empirical ML/predictive study; it is a published PISA 2022 results factsheet. Therefore, fields related to ML techniques, PV handling for model estimation, missing-data imputation strategy, and structured predictive findings are intentionally absent because the document does not estimate models or report algorithmic performance metrics. The extraction is sparse for these elements by design: the factsheet focuses on descriptive statistics, proficiency benchmarks, and subgroup comparisons using OECD’s standard PISA reporting tables.
